Case studies · anonymized

Case study · First new account · Ontario

De-icer manufacturing — a new account in a corrosive, seasonal operation

The challenge

A de-icer manufacturer in Ontario — my first new account at BDI — runs manufacturing equipment in a corrosive environment, with seasonal demand and a need for reliable component availability. When production peaks, the equipment has to keep running, and the components behind it have to be there.

My involvement

  • Identifying the industrial components the operation requires
  • Cross-referencing manufacturer part numbers across brands
  • Sourcing specialized and OEM components that don’t sit in standard catalogues
  • Comparing supplier pricing and lead times before the order goes out
  • Supporting the account’s ongoing requirements as they come up

The takeaway

Understanding the application matters as much as identifying the part — the environment a component runs in decides whether the “right” part number is actually the right part.

Case study · Bearing identification

Identifying a replacement bearing from dimensions alone

The challenge

A replacement bearing was needed with no usable part number to work from — just the bearing itself and its measurements: a 13 mm bore, 32 mm outside diameter, 10 mm wide (13×32×10).

Working it through

That 32×10 envelope is the 6201 family — but a standard 6201 has a 12 mm bore, not 13 mm. The extra millimetre on the bore makes it the non-standard variant, 6201-13. Quoting the standard number off the envelope alone would have put a bearing on the customer’s shaft that doesn’t fit it.

The takeaway

Dimensions identify the bearing — but every dimension has to be checked. The bore is the one that separates a standard catalogue number from the variant that actually fits.

Product areas I work in

BDI Canada line card

Bearings

Support rotating shafts and carry radial and axial loads while keeping friction low — ball and roller bearings, mounted units, precision machine-tool bearings, linear guides and shafting.

Common applicationsMounted units on conveyors, precision bearings in machine tools, linear guides in automation, general shaft support across plant equipment.

How to identify oneMeasure the three dimensions — bore, outside diameter, width — then confirm the type, sealing or shielding, and internal clearance. Dimensions alone can hide non-standard variants, so every measurement gets checked before a number is quoted.

Questions to askWhat shaft does it sit on, and what housing does it fit? Sealed, shielded or open? What speed and load does it see — and how did the old one fail?

Power transmission

Transfers power from a motor or drive to the equipment it runs — couplings (including CENTAFLEX), belts, chain and sprockets, gearboxes and drive components.

Common applicationsCouplings and drives for pumps, conveyors, mixers, fans and packaging lines.

How to identify oneFor a coupling: type, both shaft bores and keyways, and the torque it carries. For belts: profile and length markings. For chain: pitch and strand count. The drive layout decides which details matter.

Questions to askWhat is it driving, and at what power and speed? How much misalignment is in the setup? Is the flexible element or spider needed as well — or just the hubs?

Hydraulics & pneumatics

Moves and controls power through pressurized fluid or air — pumps, valves, cylinders, motors, hose and fittings, including Bosch Rexroth hydraulics and pneumatics.

Common applicationsCylinders, pumps and valves for presses, material handling, machine tools and plant equipment.

How to identify oneStart with the function — pump, valve, cylinder or motor — then port sizes and thread types, pressure rating, and any nameplate or casting numbers. Configuration (mounting, spool or porting pattern) has to match, not just size.

Questions to askWhat pressure and flow does the system run at? What does the component drive or control? Any nameplate data or photos of the installed unit?

Seals & fluid sealing

Keeps lubricant in and contamination out of rotating and reciprocating equipment — rotary shaft seals, hydraulic seals, O-rings, seal kits and aftermarket equivalents by equipment model.

Common applicationsSeal kits for hydraulic cylinders and gearboxes, shaft seals on pumps and motors, sealing for washdown and process equipment.

How to identify oneMeasure shaft diameter, housing bore and seal width, then confirm the profile or cross-section and the material. On cylinders, the equipment model often points straight to the correct kit.

Questions to askWhat fluid is it sealing, and at what temperature and pressure? Is it a rod, piston, wiper or rotary application? Full kit, or individual seals?

Safety & identification

Protects people and keeps a plant compliant and readable — Brady lockout/tagout devices, labels, tags and signage for equipment, panels and pipework.

Common applicationsLockout/tagout for maintenance and energy isolation, labels for panels, pipes and hazardous areas, safety signage across the plant.

How to identify oneMatch the device to the energy source it isolates — breaker, valve, plug or switch — and the label to its environment: heat, chemicals, washdown or outdoor exposure decide the material.

Questions to askWhat equipment is being locked out, and how many energy sources does it have? Where will labels live, and what do they have to survive?

Fittings & fluid power

Connects tube, pipe and hose runs in hydraulic, pneumatic and process systems — tube and pipe fittings (Tubefit and others) and related fluid connectors.

Common applicationsTube and hose connections for hydraulic power units, pneumatic lines and process piping.

How to identify oneThread type and size first — NPT, BSP and metric threads are not interchangeable — then tube or hose size, material, configuration (straight, elbow, tee) and pressure rating.

Questions to askWhat does it connect to on each end? What pressure does the line see? Stainless, steel, or brass — and what’s running through it?

Knowledge Center

Product reference · identification guides

Bearings

Ball and roller bearings — what they do

Support rotating shafts and carry radial and axial loads while keeping friction low. The main families are ball bearings, roller bearings (cylindrical, spherical and tapered), mounted units, precision machine-tool bearings, and linear guides and shafting.

Common applicationsMounted units on conveyors, precision bearings in machine tools, linear guides in automation, and general shaft support across plant equipment.

Questions to askWhat shaft does it sit on, and what housing does it fit? Sealed, shielded or open? What speed and load does it see — and how did the old one fail?

Bearings

Identifying a bearing from its dimensions

With no readable part number, measure the three dimensions — bore, outside diameter and width — then confirm the bearing type, whether it is sealed, shielded or open, and the internal clearance. The dimension set usually points to a bearing family, but every dimension still has to be checked individually.

Example: a bearing measuring 13 × 32 × 10 mm sits in the 6201 size envelope (32 mm outside diameter, 10 mm wide), but a standard 6201 has a 12 mm bore. The 13 mm bore makes it the non-standard variant, 6201-13. Ordering the standard number off the envelope alone would put a bearing on the shaft that doesn’t fit it — the bore is the dimension that separates the two.

How to identify oneMeasure all three dimensions — bore, outside diameter, width — and treat any one that breaks the standard pattern as a variant to confirm, not a rounding error.

Bearings

Mounted bearing units

A mounted unit combines a bearing insert with a housing — pillow block, flange or take-up — so the shaft support bolts straight down. Identification needs the shaft size, the housing style and bolt pattern, and the locking method: setscrew, eccentric collar or adapter sleeve.

Questions to askWhat shaft size, and which housing style and footprint? How does the insert lock to the shaft? What sealing does the environment need?

Bearings

Bearing types at a glance — matching the type to the load

The bearing type decides what loads it can carry and how it handles misalignment. Deep groove ball bearings carry radial load and moderate axial load in both directions, which is why they turn up everywhere. Angular contact ball bearings are built for combined load with axial load in one direction, and are often used in matched pairs. Cylindrical roller bearings carry heavy radial load but little axial load. Spherical roller bearings carry heavy combined load and tolerate shaft misalignment. Tapered roller bearings carry heavy combined load and are normally set up in opposed pairs.

Questions to askWhich way does the load act — radial, axial, or both? Is there misalignment to absorb? Does the bearing run as supplied, or is it adjusted in a pair?

Bearings

Sealed, shielded or open — reading a bearing's closures

Closures decide how a bearing is lubricated and protected. An open bearing has no closure: it relies on the equipment's own lubrication and sealing. A shielded bearing carries metal shields that keep larger contamination out while leaving the bearing open to the surrounding oil or grease. A sealed bearing has contact rubber seals that retain its own grease fill and exclude contamination — the usual choice where re-lubrication isn't practical. Designations commonly use suffix letters to show which closure is fitted, but suffix conventions vary by maker, so they are confirmed against that maker's system.

How to identify oneLook at the bearing's faces: exposed rolling elements means open, a metal disc means shielded, and a rubber-lipped disc that touches the inner ring means sealed.

Bearings

Bearing failure signs — reading what the old bearing says

A failed bearing usually records why it failed. Flaking or spalling on a raceway points to fatigue or overload. Evenly spaced dents point to impact damage in handling or mounting. Discoloration points to overheating, and pitting with rust points to water or contamination getting in. Damage concentrated on one side can point to misalignment. Reading the pattern before fitting the replacement matters: a like-for-like swap into the same conditions usually repeats the failure.

Questions to askIs the damage even all the way around, or concentrated on one side? Any discoloration, rust or denting? How was it lubricated — and how did it sound before it failed?

Power Transmission

Couplings — identifying what you have

For a coupling: the type, both shaft bores and keyways, and the torque it carries. Flexible couplings — including the CENTAFLEX range — absorb misalignment and shock through an elastic element; rigid and metallic types don’t, so the type has to match the drive, not just the shaft sizes.

Common applicationsCouplings and drives for pumps, conveyors, mixers, fans and packaging lines.

Questions to askWhat is it driving, and at what power and speed? How much misalignment is in the setup? Is the flexible element or spider needed as well — or just the hubs?

Power Transmission

Idler sprockets vs. finished-bore drive sprockets

Both run on roller chain of the same pitch, but they do opposite jobs. A drive sprocket has a finished bore with a keyway — usually with set screws — so it locks to the shaft and transmits torque. An idler sprocket has a bearing pressed into its bore: it spins freely on a fixed shaft or stud and only guides or tensions the chain. It transmits no torque.

To tell them apart, look at the bore. A keyway and set screws mean drive. A smooth bore with a visible bearing — inner race, seals or shields — means idler. For an idler, the dimension that matters is the bearing’s bore, which is the shaft or stud it rides on; for a drive sprocket it’s the finished bore and keyway size. Ordering one in place of the other leaves a sprocket that either free-wheels on a drive shaft or can’t spin on its stud.

How to identify oneCheck the bore first: keyway and set screws = drive sprocket; pressed-in bearing = idler. Then confirm the chain pitch and tooth count, which both types share.

Power Transmission

Belts and chain — reading the markings

For belts, the profile and length markings printed on the belt identify it — the section and length of a V-belt, or the pitch and width of a synchronous (timing) belt. For roller chain, measure the pitch (pin-to-pin distance) and count the strands — single, duplex or triplex — and note whether it is ANSI or ISO/BS standard, as the two are not interchangeable.

Questions to askBelt: which profile, and what length? Chain: what pitch, how many strands, ANSI or ISO/BS?

Power Transmission

Gear reducers — reading the nameplate

A gearbox is identified from its nameplate first: maker and model, ratio, input rating, mounting arrangement and service factor. The ratio tells you how much the input speed is reduced and the torque multiplied. Off the nameplate, confirm the input and output shaft sizes, which way the output turns, and how the unit mounts — foot, flange or shaft-mounted. Two reducers with the same ratio are not interchangeable if the shafts, mounting or output rotation differ.

How to identify onePhotograph the nameplate, then measure the input and output shafts and sketch the mounting footprint and output rotation.

Power Transmission

Roller chain wear — elongation and sprocket teeth

Chain doesn't really stretch — it elongates as the pins and bushings wear, so the pitch effectively grows and the chain starts to ride higher on the sprocket teeth. That mismatch wears the teeth into a hooked profile, and hooked teeth then accelerate chain wear in return. The pair are usually assessed together: a new chain on hooked sprockets, or new sprockets under a worn chain, wears out quickly. Lubrication and slack tell much of the story — dry, rusty chain on hooked teeth means the drive ran worn for some time.

How to identify oneCheck for stiff links and excess slack that adjustment can't take up, and look at the tooth profile — symmetrical teeth, or hooked, one-sided wear.

Power Transmission

Belt drive wear — what belts and sheaves show

V-belts wear in the grooves as much as on the belt itself. Cracking and hardening point to age and heat; glazing — a shiny, hard surface — points to slipping; fraying or uneven wear across a multi-belt set points to misalignment or a damaged groove. Belts in a matched set share the load, which is why a set is replaced as a set rather than one belt at a time. Sheave grooves wear too: a worn groove lets the belt sit too deep and slip, so the groove condition is checked alongside the belt.

Questions to askOne belt or a matched set? Any cracking, glazing or fraying? Are the sheave grooves worn, and are the sheaves aligned?

Seals

Rotary shaft seals, hydraulic seals and O-rings

Seals keep lubricant in and contamination out of rotating and reciprocating equipment. The range covers rotary shaft (oil) seals, hydraulic rod and piston seals, wipers, O-rings, and complete seal kits — including aftermarket kits matched by equipment model.

Common applicationsSeal kits for hydraulic cylinders and gearboxes, shaft seals on pumps and motors, sealing for washdown and process equipment.

Questions to askWhat fluid is it sealing, and at what temperature and pressure? Is it a rod, piston, wiper or rotary application? Full kit, or individual seals?

Seals

Identifying a seal — lip form matters as much as dimensions

Start with the three dimensions — shaft diameter, housing bore and seal width — then look at the lip. Lip form decides what the seal actually does: a single lip with a garter spring retains oil or grease on a rotating shaft, an added dust lip keeps contamination out, and other lip arrangements handle different exclusion and pressure duties. Two seals with identical dimensions and different lip forms are not interchangeable.

Material matters the same way: nitrile (NBR) covers most oil and grease duty, while FKM (fluoroelastomer) suits higher temperatures and more aggressive fluids. A seal isn’t identified until the profile or cross-section, the lip arrangement, the presence of a garter spring, and the material are all confirmed alongside the dimensions.

How to identify oneMeasure shaft, bore and width — then record the lip form (single, double, dust lip), garter spring or not, and the material before treating it as a match.

Seals

Seal kits — the equipment-model route

On hydraulic cylinders, identifying seals one by one isn’t always necessary: seal kits are catalogued by equipment model, so the machine and cylinder model often point straight to the correct kit — rod, piston and wiper seals and wear rings together. When there’s no model to work from, each seal is measured and its profile identified individually.

Questions to askFull kit, or individual seals? If it’s a cylinder application, what are the equipment make and model?

Seals

Seal materials at a glance — NBR, FKM, silicone and PTFE

Material decides what a seal survives. Nitrile (NBR) is the general-purpose choice for petroleum oils and greases. FKM fluoroelastomer handles higher temperatures and more aggressive chemicals, where nitrile would harden or swell. Silicone tolerates a wide temperature range but tears more easily and is a poor match for many oils. PTFE resists almost all chemicals and runs with low friction, but it isn't elastic like rubber, so it seals differently. The wrong material often looks right dimensionally — then swells, hardens or cracks in service.

Questions to askWhat fluid, and over what temperature range? Any chemical exposure or washdown? What did the old seal look like — swollen, hardened or cracked?

Seals

O-rings — sizing and material basics

An O-ring is identified by two dimensions — its inside diameter and its cross-section (thickness) — along with its material. It seals by being slightly compressed in its groove, so the groove's condition matters as much as the ring's: a nicked, twisted or flattened ring, or a scored groove, leaks even at the right size. Material follows the same logic as other seals: nitrile for general oil duty, FKM where heat or chemicals demand it. A removed O-ring that has taken a flat set or swelled out of shape is telling you about the duty it saw.

How to identify oneMeasure the inside diameter and cross-section without stretching the ring, and check whether it has swelled or flattened compared with a fresh, round profile.

Seals

Inside a hydraulic cylinder — rod, piston and wiper seals

Each seal position in a cylinder does a different job. The rod seal keeps pressurized fluid inside as the rod strokes. The wiper (scraper) at the rod opening keeps dirt and moisture from being drawn in as the rod retracts. The piston seal separates the two pressure sides of the piston, so the cylinder can push and pull. Wear rings guide the piston and rod and keep metal from contacting the tube. The symptom points to the position: leaking at the rod is the rod seal, drifting under load is the piston seal bypassing, and contamination getting in starts at the wiper.

Questions to askIs it leaking at the rod, or drifting under load? Is contamination getting past the wiper? A kit for the whole cylinder, or one position only?

Hydraulics/Fluid Power

Hydraulic and pneumatic components — function first

Start with the function — pump, valve, cylinder or motor — then port sizes and thread types, pressure rating, and any nameplate or casting numbers. Configuration (mounting, spool or porting pattern) has to match, not just size.

Common applicationsCylinders, pumps and valves for presses, material handling, machine tools and plant equipment.

Questions to askWhat pressure and flow does the system run at? What does the component drive or control? Any nameplate data or photos of the installed unit?

Hydraulics/Fluid Power

Tube and pipe fittings — thread type first

Thread type and size come first — NPT, BSP and metric threads are not interchangeable, and forcing a mismatch damages both sides of the connection. Then confirm the tube or hose size, the material, the configuration (straight, elbow, tee) and the pressure rating.

Questions to askWhat does it connect to on each end? What pressure does the line see? Stainless, steel or brass — and what’s running through it?

Hydraulics/Fluid Power

Hydraulic hose — reading the layline

A hydraulic hose announces itself on its cover: the printed line running along its length (the layline) normally carries the maker, the size, and the construction or standard type. The hose itself is built in layers — an oil-resistant inner tube, reinforcement (braid or spiral wire) that carries the pressure, and a cover that protects against abrasion and weather. When the layline has worn away, the size is confirmed from the inside diameter and the end fittings, and the construction from the hose's weight and flexibility.

How to identify oneRead the layline first. If it's gone, identify by inside diameter and fitting ends — and check the cover for abrasion worn down to the reinforcement.

Hydraulics/Fluid Power

How hose ends seal — flare, face seal and taper threads

Hydraulic connections seal in different ways, and telling them apart prevents mismatches. Tapered pipe threads seal on the thread itself. Flared connections seal metal-to-metal on a cone seat. O-ring face-seal and boss connections seal on an elastomer ring compressed against a flat face or into a port. Ends can look similar in size while sealing completely differently, so the seat — not just the thread — is what gets identified.

How to identify oneExamine the sealing surface: thread only, an angled cone seat, or a flat face with an O-ring. Then confirm the thread type and size.

Hydraulics/Fluid Power

Hydraulic cylinders — types and identification

Cylinders convert fluid pressure into linear force, and the common constructions are easy to tell apart. Tie-rod cylinders are held together by rods running the length of the barrel — common in industrial service and rebuildable. Welded cylinders have their ends welded to the barrel — more compact, and common on mobile equipment. Telescopic cylinders nest several stages for a long stroke from a short retracted length. Single-acting versus double-acting shows in the porting: pressure one way with spring or load return takes one port; pressure both ways takes two.

Questions to askTie-rod, welded or telescopic? Single or double-acting? How does it mount — and is it leaking externally, or bypassing internally?

Hydraulics/Fluid Power

Contamination control — keeping hydraulic fluid clean

Most hydraulic wear traces back to contamination: dirt, wear particles and water circulating in the fluid act like grinding compound on pumps, valves and seals. That is why systems are built around filtration — suction strainers, pressure and return-line filters, and a breather on the reservoir — and why filter elements are service items, not lifetime parts. Clean handling matters as much as the filters: new fluid is not necessarily clean fluid, and every opened line or removed cap is a chance for dirt to get in.

Questions to askWhich filters are fitted, and when were the elements last changed? Is the reservoir breather intact? Any milky fluid (water) or metallic sparkle in drained oil?

Safety

Lockout/tagout — match the device to the energy source

Lockout/tagout devices isolate equipment from its energy sources while maintenance is done. Match the device to the source it isolates — breaker, valve, plug or switch — and make sure every energy source on the machine is accounted for, not just the electrical supply.

Common applicationsLockout/tagout for maintenance and energy isolation across plant equipment.

Questions to askWhat equipment is being locked out, and how many energy sources does it have?

Safety

Labels, tags and signage — material follows environment

Match the label to where it will live: heat, chemicals, washdown and outdoor exposure decide the material and adhesive. Labels, tags and signage cover equipment identification, panels, pipes and hazardous areas across the plant.

Questions to askWhere will the labels live, and what do they have to survive?

Safety

Lockout devices — hasps, personal locks and device types

Lockout hardware matches the device to the isolating point: clamp-on and snap-on devices for circuit breakers, lockouts that enclose plugs, and gate-valve and ball-valve lockouts that cover the handle so it can't be operated. Where several people work on the same equipment, a lockout hasp lets each person apply their own personal lock — the equipment can't be re-energized until every lock is off, and each lock is removed only by the person who applied it.

Questions to askHow many isolation points, and of what types? How many people need to lock out at once? Each person's own lock, or locks keyed alike?

Safety

Stored energy — the energy that remains after shutdown

Switching off doesn't make equipment safe by itself. Stored energy can remain in pressurized hydraulic and pneumatic lines, in raised loads and suspended parts (gravity), in wound or compressed springs, and in hot surfaces or fluids. Lockout therefore includes releasing or restraining that energy — bleeding pressure, blocking or lowering raised parts — and then verifying: try the controls and check for pressure before work starts. The verify step is what catches the isolation point that was missed.

Questions to askWhat can still move, pressurize, fall or discharge after shutdown? How is each source released or blocked — and how is zero energy verified?

Safety

Pipe and equipment marking — contents and flow

Plant identification works when it's consistent: pipes marked with their contents and flow direction, valves tagged to the systems they serve, and equipment labelled to match the names used in procedures and lockout lists. A label that matches the procedure is what lets someone isolate the right line quickly — and a missing or mismatched one is a hazard in itself. Marking is planned as a system — what's marked, where, and in what wording — rather than tag-by-tag as problems are noticed.

Questions to askDo the equipment names on labels match the lockout procedures? Are pipe contents and flow direction shown where lines are worked on?

Safety

Accident-prevention tags — temporary warnings on equipment

Tags are the temporary half of safety identification: a do-not-operate tag on equipment that is faulty, under repair or locked out warns everyone who reaches for the controls. Unlike a permanent label, a tag is tied to a condition — it goes on when the condition starts, records who applied it and why, and comes off only when the condition is cleared, normally by the person who applied it. A tag alone doesn't physically prevent operation the way a lock does, which is why tags support lockout rather than replace it.

Questions to askIs the warning temporary (a tag) or permanent (a label)? Who applied it, and who may remove it? Is a lock also required?

Pumps & Valves

Pumps — confirming a replacement

A pump replacement is confirmed on more than its connections: the pump type (gear, vane or piston in hydraulic service; centrifugal in process service), displacement or flow, operating pressure, shaft rotation, mounting pattern, and port sizes and locations. A pump that bolts up but turns the wrong way, or displaces the wrong volume, is not a match.

Questions to askWhat pressure and flow does the system run at? Which way does the shaft turn? Any nameplate data — make, model, displacement?

Pumps & Valves

Valves — function, spool and porting

Valves direct, limit or regulate flow. Identify by function first — directional, pressure or flow control — then the spool or porting pattern, how the valve is actuated (solenoid, manual or pilot), port sizes and thread type, and the pressure rating. On a directional valve, the spool configuration has to match the original, not just the body size.

Questions to askWhat does the valve control, and how is it actuated? What are the port sizes, and what pressure does the system run at?

Pumps & Valves

Centrifugal vs. positive-displacement pumps

The two pump families behave oppositely, and confusing them causes damage. A centrifugal pump throws fluid outward with an impeller: flow is greatest at low resistance and falls as discharge pressure rises. A positive-displacement pump — gear, vane, piston or screw — traps a fixed volume and pushes it out on every cycle: flow stays nearly constant, and against a blocked discharge the pressure climbs until something gives, which is why these pumps need a relief valve protecting the discharge side.

How to identify oneLook for an impeller housing (a volute) versus a compact gear or piston body — and check whether the system has a discharge relief valve, which positive displacement requires.

Pumps & Valves

Pump cavitation — the gravel noise

Cavitation sounds like the pump is pumping gravel or marbles, and it means the inlet side is starved: vapour bubbles form in the low-pressure zone at the inlet and collapse violently as pressure rises, eroding the impeller or pump internals. The causes live on the suction side — a clogged strainer, an undersized or kinked suction line, fluid too thick when cold, or the reservoir level too low. It's a supply problem, not a pump-quality problem: a replacement pump cavitates the same way until the inlet condition is fixed.

Questions to askWhen did the noise start — with cold fluid, a level change, or a strainer service? Is the suction line clear and the reservoir level right?

Pumps & Valves

Relief valves — the system's pressure ceiling

A relief valve is a normally closed valve that opens at a set pressure and returns flow to tank, capping the pressure the whole system can build — every positive-displacement system depends on one. The symptoms point both ways: system-wide low pressure and slow actuators if it's stuck open or passing, overheating and noise if the pump works against it constantly. The setting is matched to what the weakest component in the system can take, not simply turned up when actuators feel weak.

Questions to askIs pressure low everywhere, or only in one function? Is the oil overheating? Has the setting been changed from the original?

Pumps & Valves

Check valves and flow controls — one-way flow and speed

Two simple valve functions appear everywhere. A check valve allows flow one way only — used to hold a load, protect a pump from reverse flow, or keep a circuit primed; pilot-operated versions can be opened for reverse flow when a load has to be lowered under control. A flow-control valve restricts flow to set an actuator's speed, often with a built-in check valve so one direction is controlled and the return flows freely. Which is fitted, and which direction it controls, decides whether a holding or speed problem is a valve issue at all.

Questions to askIs the problem holding a load, or controlling speed — and in which direction? Controlled flow one way, or both ways?

How I learn a product

My working method

Product→Application→Customer problem

Every new product line starts with the manufacturer’s own training, then how the part is actually applied in the plant, then the failure or problem the customer is trying to solve.
